q-120213.name: Question 1
q-120213.problem:
A survey asks a group of students about their eye color. The findings are summarized in the two-way frequency table below.

|  | Green | Blue | Brown | Black | Totals |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Girls | $10$ | $12$ | $8$ | $10$ | $40$ |
| Boys | $13$ | $12$ | $15$ | $20$ | $60$ |
| Totals | $23$ | $24$ | $23$ | $30$ | $100$ |

Let $B$ be the event that a randomly selected student is a **"Boy"**, and $C$ be the event that a randomly selected student has **"Brown"** eyes. Estimate $P(B\cap C).$
q-120213.worked_solution:
First, note that $B\cap C$ is the event that a randomly selected student is a boy and has brown eyes. 

To estimate the probability of $B\cap C,$ we

- find the number at the intersection of the row **"Boys"** and the column **"Brown"**, and then

- divide by the total number of data points in the table.

The number at the intersection of the row **"Boys"** and the column **"Brown"** is highlighted in the table below.

|  | Green | Blue | Brown | Black | Totals |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Girls | $10$ | $12$ | $8$ | $10$ | $40$ |
| Boys | $13$ | $12$ | $15$ | $20$ | $60$ |
| Totals | $23$ | $24$ | $23$ | $30$ | $100$ |

Dividing by the total number of data points in the table $(100),$ we get

$$
P(B\cap C)=\frac{15}{100}=\frac{3}{20}.
$$

q-74424.name: Question 2
q-74424.problem:
Dana surveys $72$ randomly chosen students at her school, asking them if they have gerbils or rabbits at home. Her findings are summarized in the two-way frequency table below.

|  | Has a rabbit | Doesn't have a rabbit | Totals |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Has a gerbil | $18$ | $12$ | $30$ |
| Doesn't have a gerbil | $6$ | $36$ | $42$ |
| Totals | $24$ | $48$ | $72$ |

Estimate the probability that a randomly chosen student at the school has a gerbil and also has a rabbit.
q-74424.worked_solution:
To estimate the probability that a randomly chosen student at the school has a gerbil and also has a rabbit, we

- find the number at the intersection of the row **"Has a gerbil"** and the column **"Has a rabbit"**, and then

- divide by the total number of data points in the table.

The number at the intersection of the row **"Has a gerbil"** and the column **"Has a rabbit"** is highlighted in the table below.

|  | Has a rabbit | Doesn't have a rabbit | Totals |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Has a gerbil | $18$ | $12$ | $30$ |
| Doesn't have a gerbil | $6$ | $36$ | $42$ |
| Totals | $24$ | $48$ | $72$ |

Dividing by the total number of data points in the table $(72),$ we get

$$
p=\frac{18}{72}=0.25.
$$

q-46814.name: Question 3
q-46814.problem:
Martin surveyed some students in a school, asking them if they have cats or dogs at home. His findings are summarized in the two-way frequency table below.

|  | Has a dog | Doesn't have a dog | Totals |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Has a cat | $6$ | $9$ | $15$ |
| Doesn't have a cat | $10$ | $7$ | $17$ |
| Totals | $16$ | $16$ | $32$ |

Estimate the probability that a randomly chosen student in the school has either a cat or a dog but not both.
q-46814.worked_solution:
To estimate the probability that a randomly chosen student in the school has either a cat or a dog but not both, we

- add up the numbers in the row **" Has a cat"** or the column **"Has a dog"** but not in their intersection, and

- divide by the total number of data points in the table.

The numbers in the row **"Has a cat"** or the column **"Has a dog"** but not in their intersection are highlighted below.

|  | Has a dog | Doesn't have a dog | Totals |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Has a cat | $6$ | $9$ | $15$ |
| Doesn't have a cat | $10$ | $7$ | $17$ |
| Totals | $16$ | $16$ | $32$ |

Adding up these numbers and then dividing by the total number of data points in the table $(32),$ we get

$$
p=\frac{9+10}{32}=\frac{19}{32}.
$$

q-47137.name: Question 4
q-47137.problem:
A randomly selected group of students from a high school were asked about their favorite sport between baseball, football, basketball, or soccer. The results of the survey are summarized in the two-way frequency table below.

|  | Baseball | Football | Basketball | Soccer | Totals |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Girls | $10$ | $19$ | $10$ | $12$ | $51$ |
| Boys | $10$ | $13$ | $20$ | $6$ | $49$ |
| Totals | $20$ | $32$ | $30$ | $18$ | $100$ |

Let $F$ be the event that a randomly selected student in the high school is a **"Girl"** whose favorite sport is **"Football"**, and $S$ be the event that a randomly selected student in the high school is a **"Girl"** whose favorite sport is **"Soccer"**. Estimate $P(F\cup S).$
q-47137.worked_solution:
First, note that $F\cup S$ is the event that a randomly selected student in the high school is a girl whose favorite sport is football or a girl whose favorite sport is soccer. 

To estimate the probability of $F\cup S,$ we

- add up the numbers in the columns **"Football"** or **"Soccer"** and the row **"Girls"**, and

- divide by the total number of data points in the table.

The numbers in the columns **"Football"** or **"Soccer"** and the row **"Girls"** are highlighted below.

|  | Baseball | Football | Basketball | Soccer | Totals |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Girls | $10$ | $19$ | $10$ | $12$ | $51$ |
| Boys | $10$ | $13$ | $20$ | $6$ | $49$ |
| Totals | $20$ | $32$ | $30$ | $18$ | $100$ |

Adding up these numbers and then dividing by the total number of data points in the table $(100),$ we get

$$
P(F\cup S)=\frac{19+12}{100}=\frac{31}{100}=0.31.
$$

q-47294.name: Question 7
q-47294.problem:
Roger surveyed $62$ Jefferson High School students. He asked them if they like biology and chemistry. His findings are summarized in the two-way frequency table below.

|  | Like biology | Doesn't like biology | Totals |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Like chemistry | $25$ | $19$ | $44$ |
| Doesn't like chemistry | $8$ | $10$ | $18$ |
| Totals | $33$ | $29$ | $62$ |

Edison High School has $500$ students. Assuming that the distribution of the results is the same in both high schools, determine the number of Edison High School students who like biology or chemistry but not both. Round your answer to the nearest integer.
q-47294.worked_solution:
To estimate the number of students who like biology or chemistry but not both, we

- add up the numbers in the row **"Like chemistry"** or the column **" Like biology"**, but not in both, and then

- divide by the total number of data points in the table.

|  | Like biology | Doesn't like biology | Totals |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Like chemistry | $25$ | $19$ | $44$ |
| Doesn't like chemistry | $8$ | $10$ | $18$ |
| Totals | $33$ | $29$ | $62$ |

Adding up these numbers and then dividing by the total number of data points in the table $(62),$ we get

$$
p=\frac{8+19}{62}=\frac{27}{62}=0.435.
$$

This represents the estimated probability that a randomly selected student likes biology or chemistry but not both.

Finally, to find the estimated number of students of Edison High School who like biology or chemistry but not both, we multiply the total number of students in the Edison High School $(500)$ by the probability above:

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =500\cdot p \\  & =500\cdot 0.435 \\  & =217.5 \\  & =218,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

q-47138.html:
Question 8
?

A group of randomly selected students from School A was asked about whether or not they use TV or the internet to access the local news. The results of the survey are summarized in the two-way frequency table below.

TV No TV Totals
Internet 90 15 105
No internet 30 15 45
Totals 120 30 150

There are 100 students in School B. Assuming that the distribution of the results is the same for both schools, estimate the number of School B students that access the local news either from TV or the internet, but not both.

a
 80
b
 70
c
 40
d
 30
e
 20
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To estimate the probability that a randomly selected student gets the local news either from TV or the internet but not both, we

  • add up the numbers in the row "No internet" or the column "TV", but not in both, and then

  • divide by the total number of data points in the table.

TV No TV Totals
Internet 90 15 105
No internet 30 15 45
Totals 120 30 150

Adding up these numbers and then dividing by the total number of data points in the table (150), we get

p=30+15150=45150=0.3.

This represents the estimated probability that a randomly selected student gets the local news from TV or the internet but not both.

Finally, to find the estimated number of students of School B that get their local news either from TV or the internet but not both, we multiply the total number of students in the school (100) by the probability above: n=100⋅p=100⋅0.3=30

q-120744.name: Question 9
q-120744.problem:
A group of randomly selected customers from a certain insurance company was asked about the type of vehicle driven and whether they received a speeding ticket in the last year. The results of the survey are summarized in the two-way frequency table below.

|  | SUV | Sport car | Totals |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Speeding ticket | $80$ | $5$ | $85$ |
| No speeding ticket | $20$ | $5$ | $25$ |
| Totals | $100$ | $10$ | $110$ |

There are $220$ drivers in another insurance company. Assuming that the distribution of the results is the same for both companies, estimate the number of drivers in the second insurance company that drive SUV or received a speeding ticket, but not both.
q-120744.worked_solution:
To estimate the probability that a randomly selected driver drives the SUV or received a speeding ticket but not both, we

- add up the numbers in the row **"Speeding ticket"** or the column **"SUV"**, but not in both, and then

- divide by the total number of data points in the table.

|  | SUV | Sport car | Totals |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Speeding ticket | $80$ | $5$ | $85$ |
| No speeding ticket | $20$ | $5$ | $25$ |
| Totals | $100$ | $10$ | $110$ |

Adding up these numbers and then dividing by the total number of data points in the table $(110),$ we get

$$
p=\frac{20+5}{110}=\frac{5}{22}.
$$

This represents the estimated probability that a randomly selected driver drives an SUV or received a speeding ticket but not both.

Finally, to find the estimated number of drivers in the second company that drive SUVs or received a speeding ticket, but not both, we multiply the total number of drivers in the company $(220)$ by the probability above:

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =220\cdot p \\  & =220\cdot \frac{5}{22} \\  & =50\end{aligned}
$$
